summary: Two life-size black-and-gold kings stood guard either side of the sealed burial chamber door, and caught Carter's first candlelight.
look: Two life-size wooden figures of the king, coated black, with gilded headdress, collar, kilt, sandals, mace and staff. They are a pair but not twins: one wears the striped nemes headcloth, the other the rounded khat headdress. Each strides forward on the left foot, eyes inlaid and rimmed in gold.
story:
When Carter first looked into the Antechamber in November 1922, these two loomed out of the dark facing each other on either side of a plastered, sealed doorway in the north wall. He guessed at once that something important lay behind it. Some think they were simply guardians; inscriptions on their kilts identify them with the king's ka, the life force that needed a body to live in.

The black is not skin colour. Black was the colour of the fertile Nile mud, of Osiris and of resurrection. To be black was to be reborn.

The doorway between them was officially opened on 16 February 1923, revealing the burial chamber and the first gilded shrine. But there is a twist. Many historians believe that on the night of 26 November 1922, after an unauthorised visit to the Antechamber, Carter, Lord Carnarvon and his daughter Lady Evelyn Herbert crawled through a small hole at the bottom of that sealed wall, saw what lay inside, and crawled back out. In Carter's official photographs a basket lid and a bundle of reeds lean against the foot of the wall, just where a patched hole would be. Carter never admitted the visit.

Try to picture them in their original place: two dark sentries in a cramped room heaped with gilded furniture, still on duty after 3,000 years.
details: Compare the headdresses: the striped nemes on one, the plain rounded khat on the other.
Look at the eyes, inlaid and rimmed in gold, which caught the light of Carter's candle.
Find the gilded kilts: their front panels carry the inscriptions identifying the figures with the king's ka.
Note the left foot forward, the mace in one hand and the long staff in the other.
fun_fact: In Carter's photos of the sealed doorway, a basket lid and some reeds sit conveniently at the guardians' feet, just where many suspect the hole from the secret first-night visit was patched.
narration: These two black and gold figures are the guardians, and they were among the first things Howard Carter saw by candlelight in November 1922. They stood facing each other on either side of a sealed, plastered doorway in the Antechamber: life-size images of the king, striding forward with a mace and a tall staff. Look at their heads. One wears the striped nemes headcloth, the other the plain rounded khat. Their kilts carry inscriptions linking them to the king's ka, his life force, which needed a body to live in. And the black is not skin colour. Black was the colour of the fertile Nile mud, of Osiris and of rebirth. To be black was to come back to life. Carter knew at once that something important lay behind the wall between them. It was officially opened on 16 February 1923, revealing the burial chamber. But many historians suspect that on the very first night, Carter, Lord Carnarvon and his daughter Lady Evelyn squeezed through a small hole at the bottom of that wall, took a look, and crawled back out. In Carter's photographs, a basket lid and a bundle of reeds sit against that exact spot, rather conveniently. Carter never admitted it. Now look at their faces, and at the gold rims around their eyes, and imagine them catching the flame of his candle.

summary: Six chariots found taken apart in the tomb: gilded state cars covered in bound enemies, and lighter ones built to be driven.
look: The chariots stand reassembled: light wooden bodies, six-spoked wheels and a long pole for a pair of horses. The two richest, which Carter called the state chariots, are covered in gold and glass inlay; look for rows of bound foreign captives on their panels. The plainer ones were working vehicles, probably for hunting or driving out.
story:
Carter found six chariots, all dismantled: four in the Antechamber, piled in the south-east corner, and two in the Treasury. They are made of wood, bronze, gold, linen and leather. The wheels have six spokes and flexible wooden rims that worked like tyres, and the bearings were greased with animal fat. A study in 2000 found the wheels, spokes and bearings so well designed that they compared them to European carts of the nineteenth century.

Carter noted that the two most decorated chariots did not seem to have been used before they went into the tomb. On one, glass-inlaid feathers, spirals and rosettes frame a solar falcon, cobras and the names of the king and queen, and below them foreign captives are tied around the symbol for the union of the Two Lands: the king's enemies held down forever.

So was the boy king a charioteer? His tomb was full of bows, shields and throwing sticks, and the painted box shows him in battle and on the hunt, but royal art always showed kings winning. Scans of his mummy show a broken leg, and one theory blames a chariot accident. Nobody can prove it.

For decades the chariots were split between museums; the last, from the Military Museum in the Citadel, arrived here in 2018.
details: Count the spokes: six per wheel, light and springy, built for speed.
On the gilded state chariots, find the bound captives tied around the sign for the union of the Two Lands.
Look for the king's and queen's names near the solar falcon on the richest chariot body.
Compare a gilded state chariot with a plain one: one for parades, one for driving.
fun_fact: Engineers who studied the wheels and bearings in 2000 compared them to European carts of the 1800s: 3,300-year-old suspension that still impresses.
narration: Here are Tutankhamun's chariots. Howard Carter found six of them, all taken apart: four piled in a corner of the Antechamber and two in the Treasury. They are wood, bronze, gold, linen and leather, with flexible wooden rims and bearings greased with animal fat. Engineers who studied them in 2000 compared the design to European carts of the 1800s. The two richest, which Carter called the state chariots, may never have been driven at all. Among their gold and glass, find foreign captives tied around the sign for the union of Egypt: enemies held down forever. So was this boy king, often imagined as frail, a charioteer? His tomb was full of bows, shields and hunting gear, and scans of his mummy show a broken leg, which one theory blames on a chariot crash. Nobody can prove it. One of them spent decades at the Military Museum in the Citadel, and arrived here only in 2018. Now crouch a little and count the spokes on one wheel: six, light and springy, built for speed.

summary: Three gilded couches shaped as a lioness, a cow and a hippo-crocodile: the 'strange animals' Carter saw first by candlelight.
look: Each couch is a long gilded frame whose sides are the body of an animal, with heads at the front and tails behind. One is a lioness, one a cow with a sun disc between lyre-shaped horns and a spotted hide, and the third a hippopotamus with crocodile features, its jaws open on ivory teeth and a tongue. They stood in a row against the west wall of the Antechamber, piled with boxes.
story:
When Carter first peered into the tomb, he described the room emerging slowly from the darkness: 'strange animals, statues, and gold, everywhere the glint of gold'. The strange animals were these heads, catching the candlelight.

The couches carry the names of goddesses, usually read as Isis-Mehtet for the lioness, Mehet-Weret for the cow and Ammut for the hippo creature. Mehet-Weret, 'the great flood', is the heavenly cow who lifts the newborn sun into the sky. All three are mothers and protectors linked to the sun's rebirth.

Nobody slept on them. Most Egyptologists think they served in the funeral rituals, perhaps in the embalming or in the Opening of the Mouth, the rite that gave the dead back their senses, carrying the king, like the sun, through the night towards morning.

Underneath them the Antechamber was crammed with more objects. Tucked under the hippo couch, Carter found the golden throne.
details: Compare the three heads: lioness, cow with a sun disc between her horns, and the hippo-crocodile with open jaws.
Look inside the hippo creature's mouth for the ivory teeth and the tongue.
On the cow couch, notice the spotted hide of the heavenly cow.
Walk along one side: the animal's whole body, from head to hind legs, forms the side of the bed.
fun_fact: Under the hippo couch, Carter found Tutankhamun's golden throne, shoved underneath among the clutter like a chair under a bed.
narration: These three gilded couches were among the first things Howard Carter made out when he peered into the tomb by candlelight. He wrote of strange animals, statues and gold, everywhere the glint of gold. The strange animals were these heads. The couches are shaped as animals: a lioness, a cow with a sun disc between her horns, and a creature that is part hippopotamus, part crocodile. They stood in a row against the west wall of the Antechamber, piled high with boxes. Their inscriptions name goddesses, among them the great heavenly cow who lifted the newborn sun into the sky. Nobody slept on these. Most Egyptologists think they were used in the funeral rituals, perhaps the Opening of the Mouth, which gave the dead king back his senses. Each animal is a protector who carries the sun, and the king, through the night towards the dawn. And shoved under the hippo couch, Carter found the golden throne. Now go to the hippo creature and look into its open jaws: ivory teeth and a tongue, ready to bite anything evil.

summary: A wooden chest painted with the finest miniatures in the tomb: the king in his chariot crushing Syrians, Nubians and lions in tiny detail.
look: The chest is wood, covered with a thin coat of plaster and painted. On the long sides the king charges in his chariot, against Syrians on one side and Nubians on the other; on the curved lid he hunts lions and desert animals. On the ends he appears as a sphinx trampling his enemies. Get close: the details are tiny.
story:
Carter found the box in the Antechamber and regarded it as one of the finest works of art in the whole tomb. Few have disagreed. The painter worked at miniature scale: single arrows in flight, the plumes and harness of the horses, the hair of the enemy, the agony of a speared lion.

The battle scenes follow a fixed recipe. The king, alone and gigantic in his chariot, charges; the enemy collapses into a tangled heap; his own army, tiny and orderly, follows behind. Whether Tutankhamun ever led a charge is another question. His reign did see military campaigns in Nubia and the Near East, but Egyptian royal art showed every king winning, whatever really happened.

The box was packed with the king's belongings, among them clothes and sandals. It took Carter's team weeks to empty, because the fabrics were so fragile that each layer had to be recorded and strengthened before it could be lifted. That kind of patience with fragile finds was unusual for the 1920s.
details: On the long sides, compare the enemies: bearded Syrians on one side, Nubians on the other, each with their own dress.
On the lid, find the lions pierced by arrows and the desert animals fleeing the chariot.
On the ends, look for the king as a sphinx trampling his enemies.
Bring your face close to a horse: the plumes and harness straps are painted with an almost single-hair brush.
fun_fact: The whole battle is a formula: one giant king, a heap of tangled enemies, a tidy little army behind. Egyptian war art never showed a defeat.
narration: This modest-looking wooden chest holds some of the finest painting in all of Tutankhamun's tomb, and Carter himself rated it among the best works of art he found. Get close, because everything is in miniature. On the long sides, the king in his chariot charges into battle: Syrians on one side, Nubians on the other, collapsing into a tangled heap of bodies, while his tiny army follows in neat rows. On the curved lid, he hunts lions and desert animals instead. And on the ends he becomes a sphinx, trampling his enemies. Did the boy king really fight like this? Probably not like this. His reign did see campaigns in Nubia and the Near East, but royal art showed every king winning, every time. The box was found in the Antechamber packed with the king's clothes and sandals, and it took Carter's team weeks to empty, lifting fragile fabrics one layer at a time. Now look closely at one of the horses: you can see the plumes on its head, the harness straps, and, if you look really closely, single arrows in flight.

summary: A black jackal on a golden chest guarded the Treasury door, and was found dressed in a linen shirt dated to year 7 of Akhenaten.
look: Anubis lies like a watchful dog on a gilded chest shaped like a temple gateway, mounted on a sledge with carrying poles; poles included, it is 2.735 metres long. The jackal, 60 centimetres tall, is wood painted black, with gold leaf inside the ears and on the eyebrows, eye rims and collar, eyes of calcite and obsidian set in gold, and silver claws.
story:
He lay in the open doorway between the Burial Chamber and the Treasury, facing west, with the great canopic shrine behind him. While the burial chamber was being cleared, Carter boarded up that doorway; the Treasury was only emptied in the 1926-27 season, and Carter described the jackal in his journal on 23 October 1926. Harry Burton's photograph of him in the doorway, still draped in linen, is one of the great images of the excavation.

Anubis was dressed. Under everything was fine linen gauze tied at the neck; over it hung two thin garlands of blue lotus and cornflowers; and on top lay a linen shirt with an ink inscription dating it to year 7 of Akhenaten. Between his front paws lay an ivory writing palette inscribed for Meritaten, Akhenaten's eldest daughter.

The shrine is also a chest. Four small trays held ritual objects, among them faience pieces, figures of Ra and Thoth, a wax bird, resin and two calcite cups of salt and natron. A larger compartment held jewellery, wrapped and sealed, which ancient robbers had disturbed.

In front of him lay a magic brick of unfired clay, with a text Carter quoted: 'It is I who hinder the sand from choking the secret chamber.' The press of the 1920s turned this into the curse of the pharaohs. The real words only keep out the sand. His pose is the hieroglyph that writes his name, with the title 'Anubis over the mysteries'.
details: Look down at his front paws: the claws are silver.
Find the gold leaf inside the ears and on the collar, bright against the black.
On the sides of the chest, look for djed pillars and tyet knots, symbols of Osiris and Isis.
Follow the carrying poles: 2.735 metres long overall, this was carried in the funeral procession.
fun_fact: When the jackal was cleared, an ivory writing palette belonging to Meritaten, Akhenaten's eldest daughter, lay between his paws: a family hand-me-down for a god.
narration: This black jackal is Anubis, god of embalming and guardian of the dead, and for more than 3,000 years he lay exactly like this in the doorway of the Treasury, facing west, on guard. Behind him stood the golden canopic shrine with the king's organs. He is wood, painted black, with gold inside his ears and on his eyebrows and collar, eyes of white calcite and black obsidian set in gold, and claws of silver. He rests on a gilded chest shaped like a temple gateway, mounted on a sledge with carrying poles, so he was probably carried in the funeral procession. When Carter's team cleared him in October 1926, he was dressed. A fine linen veil was tied at his neck, two thin garlands of blue lotus and cornflowers hung round it, and over everything lay a linen shirt with an ink date: year 7 of Akhenaten, probably the young king's father. Between his paws was an ivory writing palette belonging to Meritaten, Akhenaten's eldest daughter. Family hand-me-downs, even for a god. In front of him lay a clay brick with a spell: it is I who hinder the sand from choking the secret chamber. Newspapers spun words like these into the famous curse. They only keep out the sand. Now look down at his front paws, and find the silver claws.

summary: Four gilded shrines nested like Russian dolls filled the burial chamber wall to wall; an unbroken seal inside told Carter no robber had reached the king.
look: The shrines are great boxes of gilded wood, one inside the other, the biggest the size of a small room and the smallest just large enough for the sarcophagus. Every surface is covered in gods, spells and protective signs; the outermost is inlaid with blue faience djed pillars and tyet knots. Between the outer shrine and the second stood a wooden frame hung with a linen pall spangled with bronze rosettes.
story:
The burial chamber measures about 6.4 by 4 metres, and the shrines filled it almost to the walls. They were made in prefabricated gilded panels, carried down the corridor and assembled inside. Carpenters had marked which piece went where, and Carter noticed that the funeral crew had put some of them together in the wrong order, in a hurry.

When the doors of the outer shrine were opened in 1923, the pall on its frame appeared, and behind it the doors of the second shrine, tied with cord and closed with a clay seal that was still intact. That seal told Carter that the robbers who had twice entered the tomb had never reached the king.

The texts are important. The outermost shrine carries the earliest known copy of the Book of the Heavenly Cow. In it the sun god Ra, grown old, finds humans plotting against him and sends his Eye, as a raging goddess, to destroy them; then he relents and saves the rest by flooding the fields with beer dyed red to look like blood. The goddess drinks, gets drunk and forgets her massacre. The second shrine bears a cryptic funerary text found nowhere else, related to texts in the tombs of Ramesses VI and Ramesses IX. All four carry extracts from the Book of the Dead, and the third adds passages from the Amduat, the guide to the night journey of the sun.

Taking them apart in that cramped space cost Carter's team weeks before they could reach the stone sarcophagus.
details: On the outermost shrine, find the blue faience inlays: the djed pillar of Osiris and the tyet knot of Isis, repeated.
If the pall frame is shown, look for the bronze rosettes scattered over the linen like stars.
Look at the doors and their bolts: the second shrine's doors were tied with cord and sealed.
Scan the panels for columns of text: the outermost carries the oldest Book of the Heavenly Cow.
Check corners and joints for carpenters' marks that told the funeral crew how to assemble them.
fun_fact: The Book of the Heavenly Cow on the outer shrine tells how the sun god stopped a goddess's massacre of humanity by getting her drunk on beer dyed red to look like blood.
narration: These golden boxes are the four shrines that surrounded Tutankhamun's sarcophagus, one inside the other like Russian dolls. The biggest is the size of a small room, and the burial chamber, about 6 metres by 4, was so full that there was barely space to squeeze between shrine and wall. They were made as panels of gilded wood, carried down the corridor and assembled inside. Carpenters had marked which piece went where, and Carter noticed the funeral crew put some of them together in the wrong order, in a hurry. When the doors of the outer shrine were opened in 1923, Carter found a frame draped with a linen pall spangled with bronze rosettes, like stars. Behind it, the doors of the second shrine were tied with cord and closed with a clay seal, still unbroken. That seal told him no robber had ever reached the king. Now the texts. The outermost shrine carries the oldest known copy of the Book of the Heavenly Cow. In it, the sun god, old and tired of rebellious humans, sends his fierce Eye to destroy them, then changes his mind and saves the rest by flooding the fields with beer dyed red like blood. The goddess drinks it, gets drunk and forgets her rampage. Now look at the sides of the outermost shrine and find the blue inlays: pillars and knots, the symbols of Osiris and Isis, repeated like protective wallpaper.

summary: A dagger forged from iron that fell from the sky: its blade's nickel and cobalt match meteorites, in an age when iron was worth more than gold.
look: Two daggers were found in the mummy's wrappings: one with a gold blade, and this one with an iron blade that has barely rusted. The handle is gold, decorated with fine granulation and inlaid bands and topped by a knob of rock crystal; the gold sheath ends in a jackal's head. Look for the dull grey of the blade beside all that gold.
story:
Carter found two daggers in the wrappings in 1925, one with a gold blade and one with iron. The iron one lay along the king's right thigh.

In Tutankhamun's time Egyptians did not smelt iron; the earliest evidence of iron smelting in Egypt dates from the sixth century BC. Iron was rare, used for gifts, rituals and ornaments, and by some accounts more precious than gold. Royal gifts of iron are recorded in the reign of Amenhotep III, just before him.

In 2016 an Italian and Egyptian team analysed the blade with X-ray fluorescence, which does not touch the object. It contains about 11 percent nickel and 0.6 percent cobalt. Iron made from ore before the nineteenth century never exceeds about 4 percent nickel; iron meteorites typically hold between 5 and 35 percent, and the blade's nickel-to-cobalt ratio matches them. The researchers compared it with a meteorite found in 2000 near Marsa Matruh, on your road to Siwa.

Who made it? A 2022 Japanese-led study found signs of forging at relatively low temperature and traces of lime plaster in the adhesive of the hilt, a technique not used in Egypt at the time. That points to a foreign workshop, possibly in Mitanni, in northern Syria. One of the Amarna letters, from King Tushratta of Mitanni to Amenhotep III, lists among his wedding gifts 'one dagger, the blade of iron, the hilt of tooled gold', and a second iron dagger besides. It is tempting to think one of them ended up with his grandson, though nobody can prove it.

The tomb held 19 iron objects in all, including a miniature headrest found inside the mask.
details: Find the iron blade: grey and remarkably free of rust after more than 3,300 years.
Look at the gold handle: fine granulation and inlaid bands, topped by a knob of rock crystal.
On the gold sheath, find the jackal's head at the tip.
Compare it with its companion, the dagger with a gold blade, also found on the mummy.
fun_fact: Ancient Egyptian texts sometimes called iron objects 'stars'. For this dagger, that was simply accurate.
narration: This little dagger may be the most out-of-this-world object in the museum, quite literally. Howard Carter found it in 1925 inside the mummy's wrappings, lying along the king's right thigh. The handle is gold, decorated with tiny gold granules and topped by a knob of rock crystal, and the gold sheath ends in a jackal's head. But look at the blade. It is iron, and it has barely rusted. In Tutankhamun's day, Egyptians did not smelt iron; that came some 700 years later. Iron was rare and precious, given as royal gifts, and by some accounts worth more than gold. Ancient texts even called iron objects stars. In 2016 scientists scanned the blade with X-rays without touching it. It contains about 11 percent nickel and some cobalt, a recipe that iron smelted from ore at that time never has, but iron meteorites do. The blade was made from a meteorite. A 2022 study then found traces of lime plaster in the glue of the handle, unusual in Egypt at the time, pointing to a foreign workshop, possibly in Mitanni, in northern Syria. And one of the Amarna letters, from King Tushratta of Mitanni to Tutankhamun's grandfather, lists a gift: a dagger with a blade of iron and a hilt of gold. Now look at the dull grey of the blade next to all that gold, and remember: that metal fell from the sky.

summary: The oldest working trumpets in the world were played live on BBC radio in 1939, and legend says war follows whenever they sound.
look: Two trumpets: one of silver, 57.2 centimetres long, and one of bronze or copper with a gold-alloy bell, about 7.6 centimetres shorter. Both are engraved with the gods Ra-Horakhty, Ptah and Amun, and the silver bell opens like a lotus flower carrying the king's names. The silver trumpet came with a wooden core that fitted inside it.
story:
The bronze trumpet was found in the Antechamber, in a large chest with military objects and walking sticks; the silver one turned up later in the burial chamber. They were probably military signal trumpets, sounding a single note.

On 16 April 1939 the BBC broadcast them live from Cairo to an estimated 150 million listeners. Bandsman James Tappern of the 11th Hussars had to fit a modern mouthpiece, wedged in with packing, to play them. The presenter, Rex Keating, later said the silver trumpet shattered during a rehearsal, and Alfred Lucas, the chemist who had restored the finds, was so distressed he needed hospital treatment. The trumpet was repaired. Five months later the Second World War began.

That coincidence fed a legend. A museum curator quoted in Al-Ahram said the trumpet had magical powers: whenever someone blows into it, a war occurs. Stories link a blast to the Six-Day War of 1967, another to the Gulf War, and a staff member's test a week before the upheaval of 2011. That year the bronze trumpet was stolen from the museum during the looting, and mysteriously returned weeks later.

Modern trumpeters have coaxed three notes out of them: one poor, one clear, and one so forceful it could destroy the instrument. They are unlikely ever to be played again.
details: Compare the two: silver, 57.2 centimetres, and bronze with a gold-alloy bell, a little shorter.
On the silver bell, look for the lotus petals and the king's two cartouches.
Find the engraved gods: falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty, Ptah in his skullcap, and Amun with tall plumes.
If it is displayed, look for the decorated wooden core that slid inside the silver trumpet.
fun_fact: The 1939 recording survives, and the BBC still replays it: most recently on its Breakfast programme in July 2023.
narration: These are the oldest working trumpets in the world: one of silver, one of bronze with a gold bell, both engraved with the gods Ra-Horakhty, Ptah and Amun. They were probably army signal trumpets. Carter found the bronze one in a chest in the Antechamber and the silver one in the burial chamber. On 16 April 1939 the BBC broadcast them live from Cairo to an estimated 150 million listeners. A British army bandsman, James Tappern, had to wedge in a modern mouthpiece to play them. The presenter later said the silver trumpet shattered in rehearsal, and the chemist who had restored it was so upset he went to hospital. Five months after the broadcast, the Second World War began. And so a legend was born: whenever someone blows Tutankhamun's trumpet, a war follows. Stories link it to 1967 and to the Gulf War. In 2011 the bronze trumpet was stolen from the museum, and it mysteriously came back weeks later. Now look at the silver bell: it opens like a lotus flower, with the king's names on it.

summary: Tutankhamun took board games into eternity: senet, a race across 30 squares that became a game of passing through the underworld.
look: Look for the game boxes: 30 squares in three rows of ten on one face, on some a second game of 20 squares on the other, and a drawer for the playing pieces. The finest is ebony and ivory on a stand with animal legs.
story:
Senet means 'passing'. Boards that may be senet appear in First Dynasty burials around 3100 BC, and the game is painted in the tomb of Hesy-Ra around 2620 BC. Two players raced their pieces along the squares, using throw sticks instead of dice. Nobody knows the exact rules; modern reconstructions disagree.

By the New Kingdom, senet had become sacred: the board was the soul's passage through the underworld. Chapter 17 of the Book of the Dead shows the dead playing against an invisible opponent, and Queen Nefertari is painted at the board in her tomb. Tutankhamun's tomb held four game boxes, so he could go on playing forever.
details: Count the squares: three rows of ten. The last few often carry special signs.
Look for the drawer in the end of the box that held the pieces and throw sticks.
Check the other face of the board for the second game, twenty squares.
fun_fact: In the Book of the Dead, the deceased plays senet against an opponent nobody can see: a board game where the rival is invisible and the prize is eternity.
narration: Tutankhamun took board games with him. These boxes are for senet, a word meaning passing. On top you will see 30 squares in three rows of ten, and on some boxes a second game of 20 squares on the other side, with a drawer for the pieces. Instead of dice, players threw flat sticks. Senet is ancient: it is painted in a tomb from about 2620 BC. By Tutankhamun's time it was more than a game. The board stood for the soul's journey through the underworld, and the Book of the Dead shows the dead playing against an invisible opponent. Look now for the little drawer in the end of a box, where the pieces were kept.

summary: More than 80 pieces of footwear, including sandals with enemies on the soles, so the king trod on his foes with every step.
look: Look for the wooden sandals with bound foreign captives on the insoles, and for the gold sandals that were found on the mummy's feet. Simpler sandals of plant fibre and leather show what the king wore every day.
story:
The tomb held more than 80 pieces of footwear, from simple sewn sandals of plant fibre to decorated shoes; a study by André Veldmeijer examined 81 of them. One wooden pair shows bound foreigners, an Asiatic and a Nubian, on the insoles: every step was a small daily conquest. On the mummy itself, the feet wore gold sandals and each toe had its own gold cap.

The feet also feed a medical argument. A 2010 study of the mummy reported a clubfoot and bone disease in the left foot and pointed to the many walking sticks in the tomb. Other experts argue the damage happened after death. The debate is open.
details: Find the sandals with bound captives on the insoles: an Asiatic and a Nubian under the royal heel.
Look for the gold sandals and the gold toe caps that were on the mummy's feet.
Notice the plain plant-fibre sandals: everyday royal footwear, not so different from anyone else's.
fun_fact: Even in death the king's toes were dressed individually: each toe and finger of the mummy had its own gold cap.
narration: Tutankhamun's tomb held more than 80 pieces of footwear, from plain sandals of plant fibre to gold. Look for the wooden pair with bound prisoners on the insoles, a foreigner from Asia and one from Nubia. Every time the king took a step, he trod on his enemies. The mummy itself wore gold sandals, and each of his toes had its own gold cap. His feet are also part of a medical puzzle. A 2010 study reported a clubfoot and bone disease in his left foot, and pointed to the many walking sticks found in the tomb. Other experts think the damage happened after death. Now find the captives on the soles, and look at their faces.

summary: A painted wooden torso of the king with no arms and a flat-topped crown: maybe a dummy for his clothes, maybe something more magical.
look: This life-size head and torso is carved in wood, plastered and painted, and ends at the waist with no arms. The king wears a flat-topped crown, and the face is young and soft. It was found in the Antechamber.
story:
Carter found the figure in the Antechamber, the room where boxes of the king's clothes were stacked, and he thought it was a mannequin: a dummy on which the king's robes or jewellery were fitted. The shape fits the idea, life-size, armless and cut off at the waist like a modern dress form. And there was plenty to dress: tunics, shirts, kilts, gloves and sandals came out of the Antechamber boxes alone.

Other Egyptologists prefer a ritual explanation, a stand-in body for the king's ka or an image used in ceremonies. Nothing written on it settles the question.

What makes it special is the face. Royal portraits are usually polished into an ideal. This one, life-size and painted, feels closer to a real young man. Compare it with the gold mask, the same features turned into a god, and with the lotus head, which shows him as a small child. Three portraits, three ages, one boy.
details: Look at the crown: flat-topped, an unusual shape among the king's many headdresses.
Notice the shoulders and chest end abruptly with no arms: exactly the shape of a dress form.
Compare the face with the gold mask: same features, but here the painted skin feels more human.
Walk round the side and look at the profile, the line of lips and chin.

narration: This painted wooden figure is a life-size head and torso of Tutankhamun, with no arms, ending at the waist, wearing a flat-topped crown. Carter found it in the Antechamber, the room stacked with furniture and boxes of clothes, and he thought it was a mannequin: a dummy on which the king's robes or jewellery were fitted. Life-size, armless, cut off at the waist, it is basically a dress form. And the tomb had plenty to dress: tunics, shirts, kilts, even gloves. Other Egyptologists suspect a ritual role, perhaps a stand-in body for the king's spirit, used in ceremonies. What makes it special is the face. Royal portraits are usually polished into perfection. This one feels closer to a real young man. You have three portraits of him in these halls: the golden mask, made as a god; the lotus head, as a little child; and this one, somewhere in between. Look now at the face from the side, at the line of the lips and the chin, and compare it in your mind with the gold mask.

summary: An alabaster cup shaped like an open lotus, whose wish for 'millions of years' ended up carved on Howard Carter's own gravestone.
look: The chalice is carved from a single piece of alabaster, 18.3 centimetres high, in the shape of a white lotus in full bloom. The handles are blue lotus flowers and buds topped by the kneeling god Heh, who holds notched palm ribs that count years, each resting on a tadpole and a shen ring. An inscription runs round the rim from a central ankh.
story:
It lay on the floor just inside the Antechamber, among the first things Carter's team saw, though not in its original place. Carter called it the Wishing Cup, because of its text.

The white lotus with its rounded petals is the cup; blue lotus flowers and buds form the handles. On each, Heh, the god of infinity, kneels on a basket, the sign for 'all', holding palm ribs notched to count years. Under each rib sits a tadpole, the hieroglyph for 100,000, on a shen ring, the sign of eternity. Together they say: endless time, forever.

The rim inscription runs two ways from a central ankh. One way gives the king's full titles. The other is the wish: may his ka live, may he spend millions of years, he who loves Thebes, sitting with his face to the north wind, his eyes beholding happiness. Alan Gardiner provided the translation for Carter's publication.

Carter clearly loved it. When he died in London in 1939, only nine people attended his funeral. His gravestone in Putney Vale Cemetery carries the cup's words: 'May your spirit live, may you spend millions of years, you who love Thebes, sitting with your face to the north wind, your eyes beholding happiness.'
